notes: The twelve sacred olives (moriai). Each carries a myth, law or historical fragment, paraphrased with its source.

moria-1.title: The second olive
moria-1.text: Pausanias was told this olive was the second ever to appear, after Athena's own on the Acropolis. When the Persians burned the Acropolis in 480, Athena's olive sprouted a new shoot a cubit long the very next day.

moria-2.title: A capital matter
moria-2.text: A landowner was prosecuted before the Areopagus for removing the stump of a sacred olive. The penalty could be exile and the loss of his property. Lysias wrote his defence.

moria-3.title: Oil for the victors
moria-3.text: Oil from the sacred olives filled the painted amphorae given as prizes at the Panathenaic games. An archon collected it from the owners of land where moriai grew.

moria-4.title: The contest for Athens
moria-4.text: Athena and Poseidon competed for the city. Poseidon struck the rock and a salt spring welled up; Athena planted the olive. The olive was judged the better gift.

moria-5.title: The tree no spear can kill
moria-5.text: The chorus of Colonus sings of the grey-leaved olive, self-renewing, a terror to enemy spears, that neither young nor old can destroy, watched by Zeus of the Moriai and Athena.

moria-6.title: Zeus of the Moriai
moria-6.text: The sacred olives had their own guardian: Zeus Morios, whose unsleeping eye watched over them alongside grey-eyed Athena.

moria-7.title: Olive wood for Epidaurus
moria-7.text: When the Epidaurians needed statues to end a famine, the Delphic oracle told them to carve them from cultivated olive wood. Athens alone had such olives, and gave them wood in return for yearly offerings.

moria-8.title: The suppliant's branch
moria-8.source: Aeschylus, Suppliants; Sophocles, Oedipus the King 3
moria-8.text: Suppliants carried olive branches wound with wool to show they came in peace and asked for protection.

moria-9.title: Beating the branches
moria-9.source: Black-figure amphora by the Antimenes Painter (British Museum)
moria-9.text: Harvesters beat the branches with long poles while a boy climbs into the tree and another gathers fallen olives from the ground, as painted on a vase of about 520 BC.

moria-10.title: Oil for body and lamp
moria-10.text: Oil fed the lamps, dressed the food, and was rubbed into athletes' skin before exercise, then scraped off with the dust using a bronze strigil.

moria-11.title: Old as the city
moria-11.text: Theophrastus noted that the olive is among the longest-lived of trees and that, cut down, it sends up new shoots from the stump.

moria-12.title: A hundred and forty jars
moria-12.text: An inscription lists the prizes: the winner of the boys' stadion race received fifty amphorae of oil, and the men's chariot race up to a hundred and forty. A fortune, from Athena's trees.
